courses.title: 1. Game Architecture & Modding Foundations
courses.summary: Understand game engine execution loops, tick cycles, ECS and OOP object models, the taxonomy of game mods (asset, script, bytecode, binary), and ethical boundaries with anti-cheat systems.
courses.expected: Compiles with C++17 (`g++ -std=c++17 mod-architecture.cpp`). Output shows the game loop dispatching events, the mod intercepting incoming damage to PlayerHero and cancelling it (GodMode), and doubling outgoing damage against DragonBoss from 40 to 80.

lessons.title: The game loop & tick lifecycle
paragraphs: At the core of every interactive game is the game loop. Unlike event-driven desktop software that sleeps until an OS event occurs, a game engine continuously loops through input processing, state updates, physics simulation, audio generation, and rendering. Updates typically occur on a fixed timestep (e.g., 50 or 60 Hz for physics) or variable timestep (rendering at the monitor's refresh rate).

Mod authors must understand when their hooks execute relative to the tick cycle. Intercepting input before physics calculation allows aim assists and movement modifications; intercepting post-physics state allows telemetry logging, camera smoothing, and UI overlays. Modifying state outside the designated tick thread can lead to race conditions, synchronization desyncs, and immediate crashes.
lessons.example: while (running) { processInput(); updatePhysics(fixedDt); updateGameLogic(dt); render(frameAlpha); }
lessons.pitfall: Executing heavy blocking operations (such as synchronous network requests or disk I/O) inside the tick loop causes severe frame rate stuttering and physics instability.

question.prompt: Why is game logic typically calculated using a fixed timestep (delta time) rather than raw frame rates?

options.text: To prevent GPU overheating during menu screens
To ensure physics and gameplay behave deterministically across different hardware and frame rates
Because C++ compilers do not support floating-point arithmetic at high frame rates

question.explanation: Fixed timesteps decouple game physics and logic from hardware rendering speed, ensuring characters jump the same distance regardless of whether the game runs at 30 FPS or 240 FPS.

lessons.title: Entities, components & memory locality
paragraphs: Older game engines relied on deep Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) inheritance hierarchies (e.g., Actor -> Pawn -> Character -> Player). Modern engines frequently adopt the Entity-Component-System (ECS) architectural pattern, where Entities are lightweight integer IDs, Components are pure plain-old-data (POD) structs, and Systems contain the iterative logic that processes matching components.

For modders, ECS engines store components in contiguous memory arrays (archetypes or sparse sets) for cache locality. Instead of navigating complex virtual pointer tables to find an object's health, an ECS mod can query the HealthComponent array directly, significantly simplifying memory scanning and batch modifications.
lessons.example: OOP: entity->getComponent<Health>()->takeDamage(10); vs ECS: for (auto [id, hp, pos] : view) { hp.value -= 10; }
lessons.pitfall: Assuming all game objects have continuous virtual method tables; in pure ECS architectures, entities have no vtables and methods live in separate stateless systems.

question.prompt: In an Entity-Component-System (ECS) architecture, what is an Entity?

options.text: A polymorphic C++ base class containing virtual update functions
A unique numeric identifier (ID) that groups associated component data
A GPU compute shader that handles matrix multiplications

question.explanation: In ECS, an entity is merely an identifier (often a 32-bit or 64-bit integer) used to index into data tables holding components.

lessons.title: Taxonomy of game mods
paragraphs: Game modifications span a spectrum of technical complexity. Content and data mods replace existing assets (textures, 3D meshes, audio, localization text) or tweak declarative tables (JSON, XML, SQLite, YAML) without changing executable code. Script mods hook into exposed runtime engines (Lua, Python, Unreal Blueprints) via official or community mod loaders.

At the deepest level, bytecode and binary mods modify the game's executable instructions. In managed environments (Unity/C#, Java), modders decompile and rewrite Intermediate Language (IL) bytecode using frameworks like BepInEx and Harmony. In native environments (C/C++), modders use dynamic binary instrumentation, DLL injection, and memory detours to patch machine code at runtime.
lessons.example: Asset Mod: replacing skin.png; Script Mod: adding quest.lua; Binary Mod: hooking TakeDamage() in game.exe.
lessons.pitfall: Modifying game executables on disk triggers hash-based integrity checks and anti-piracy validations; runtime memory patching is cleaner and non-destructive.

question.prompt: Which type of mod modifies executable machine instructions in the running game's memory space rather than swapping asset files?

options.text: Texture pack mod
Binary/runtime hook mod
Localization string mod

question.explanation: Binary or runtime hook mods alter process memory by injecting code, hooking functions, or patching machine instructions at runtime.

lessons.title: Anti-cheat systems & ethical boundaries
paragraphs: Modding single-player and cooperative sandbox games enriches player creativity and extends game longevity (e.g., Skyrim, Minecraft, Factorio). However, applying modding techniques in competitive multiplayer games undermines fair play, degrades user trust, and violates Terms of Service. Anti-cheat software operates across user space and kernel space to detect unauthorized memory access and binary tampering.

User-mode anti-cheats (like Valve Anti-Cheat / VAC) inspect process memory modules, scan for known cheat signatures, verify code section checksums, and detect unauthorized thread injection. Kernel-level anti-cheats (such as Easy Anti-Cheat, BattlEye, Vanguard) install kernel drivers to monitor process handles (`OpenProcess`), intercept page manipulation (`VirtualProtect`), and enforce hypervisor-protected code integrity (HVCI).
lessons.example: Single-player modding: creative sandboxes and offline debugging. Multiplayer anti-cheat: kernel drivers blocking OpenProcess and memory writes.
lessons.pitfall: Running debugger or memory scanner tools while connected to VAC-secured or kernel-anti-cheat multiplayer servers can result in irreversible account bans.

question.prompt: What technique do user-mode anti-cheat systems frequently use to detect binary code tampering?

options.text: Calculating cryptographic hashes of executable code sections (.text) and comparing them against disk copies
Disabling the computer's graphics card drivers during gameplay
Replacing all game C++ classes with interpreted Python scripts

question.explanation: Anti-cheat software periodically scans the `.text` executable code section of loaded game modules, checking if bytes have been modified by patches or detour jumps.

courses.title: 2. Memory Layout, Virtual Addresses & Pointer Chains
courses.summary: Master process virtual address spaces, ASLR base addresses, dynamic heap allocations, multi-level pointer dereferencing, and memory scanning algorithms.
courses.expected: Compiles with C++17 (`g++ -std=c++17 mod-memory-internals.cpp`). Output displays the multi-step pointer chain traversal through EngineModule -> GameInstance -> PlayerController -> PlayerStats, successfully overwriting health and gold, followed by scanner identification.

lessons.title: Virtual memory space & ASLR
paragraphs: Operating systems grant every modern process an isolated virtual address space (up to 4 GB in 32-bit x86, and 128 TB+ in 64-bit x64). Virtual addresses do not correspond to physical RAM chips directly; the CPU's Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates virtual pages to physical frames via page tables.

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is an OS security mitigation that randomizes the base memory address of executables and shared libraries (DLLs / .so files) every time the game launches. Modders cannot hardcode absolute addresses (e.g., `0x00401234`). Instead, they determine the module's dynamic base address at runtime and compute relative virtual addresses (RVA): `EffectiveAddress = ModuleBase + RVA`.
lessons.example: uintptr_t moduleBase = (uintptr_t)GetModuleHandleA("game.exe"); uintptr_t playerPtr = *(uintptr_t*)(moduleBase + 0x145A80);
lessons.pitfall: Hardcoding absolute memory addresses found during one game session causes instant crashes on subsequent launches due to ASLR base shifting.

question.prompt: Why do memory addresses found in one game session change when the game is restarted?

options.text: Operating systems wipe all RAM tables when games exit
Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) assigns a different base address to executable modules on each launch
Game compilers generate different machine code opcodes on every computer restart

question.explanation: ASLR randomizes module base addresses to prevent memory-corruption exploits, meaning modders must use relative offsets from module bases.

lessons.title: Memory scanning techniques
paragraphs: Memory scanners (such as Cheat Engine or custom memory utilities) locate variables by scanning readable pages of a process. The process starts with an initial scan for a known value (e.g., current player ammo = 30). Because thousands of memory addresses may hold the integer 30, the scanner records all matching addresses in a candidate list.

The player then alters the in-game value (fires a bullet -> ammo becomes 29) and performs a subsequent 'filter scan' on the candidate list. Subsequent scans can filter for decreased values, increased values, exact values, or unchanged values. For floating-point variables (such as health or coordinates), scanners apply tolerance ranges (e.g. ±0.01) to account for floating-point inaccuracies.
lessons.example: Scan 1: Health = 100 (5,000 matches) -> Take damage -> Scan 2: Health = 84 (2 matches) -> Take damage -> Scan 3: Health = 68 (1 match).
lessons.pitfall: Scanning with the wrong data type (e.g. searching for a 4-byte integer when the game stores health as a 32-bit single-precision float) produces zero results.

question.prompt: How does a memory scanner narrow down thousands of candidate addresses to find a player's ammo count?

options.text: By performing subsequent filter scans on candidate addresses after the in-game ammo value changes
By resetting the computer's CPU registers to zero
By deleting all non-game background processes

question.explanation: Changing the in-game value and filtering the previous candidate list for the new value quickly eliminates unrelated memory addresses.

lessons.title: Multilevel pointer offsets
paragraphs: Most game variables (such as player entities, enemies, and inventory items) are dynamically allocated on the heap at runtime with `new` or `malloc`. Their memory addresses change every time a new level loads. To reliably access dynamic objects across sessions, modders construct multi-level pointer paths starting from a static base address.

A static base address resides within a loaded module's data section (`.data` or `.bss`) and maintains a fixed offset from the module base. This static pointer points to a GameInstance, which contains an offset pointing to a PlayerController, which contains an offset pointing to the PlayerState. By dereferencing each pointer and adding the corresponding struct offset, the mod reliably finds the dynamic variable.
lessons.example: TargetVariable = *(*(*(ModuleBase + 0x2A10) + 0x48) + 0x100) + 0x24;
lessons.pitfall: Dereferencing a pointer chain without checking for null intermediate pointers triggers an access violation (SIGSEGV / 0xC0000005) when loading screens or transitions occur.

question.prompt: What is the primary purpose of finding a multi-level pointer chain in game modding?

options.text: To double the speed of network packet transmissions
To reliably reach dynamic heap variables from a static module offset across game restarts and level loads
To bypass the need for an operating system kernel

question.explanation: Pointer chains link a reliable, static module base address to dynamically allocated heap entities that change locations between level transitions.

lessons.title: Page protection & memory permissions
paragraphs: Process memory is partitioned into 4 KB virtual pages, each marked with access permission flags: `PAGE_READONLY`, `PAGE_READWRITE`, `PAGE_EXECUTE_READ`, or `PAGE_NOACCESS`. By default, game code sections (`.text`) are executable and readable, but write-protected to prevent code corruption and buffer-overflow exploits.

When a mod needs to patch machine instructions or write to write-protected pages, it must call the OS memory API (such as `VirtualProtect` on Windows or `mprotect` on POSIX). The mod changes the page permission to `PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE`, writes the patch, and immediately restores the original permissions to preserve process stability and avoid tripping integrity scanners.
lessons.example: DWORD oldProtect; VirtualProtect(targetAddr, size, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE, &oldProtect); *patch = 0x90; VirtualProtect(targetAddr, size, oldProtect, &oldProtect);
lessons.pitfall: Leaving memory pages permanently marked as `PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE` (RWX) is a major red flag for anti-cheat and security software, as normal game code sections should never remain writable.

question.prompt: What OS API function is used on Windows to temporarily make executable memory writable for patching?

options.text: VirtualProtect
CreateWindowEx
RegOpenKeyEx

question.explanation: VirtualProtect allows modifying page access permissions (such as granting write access to code pages) and retrieving original protection flags.

courses.title: 3. Static Analysis, Disassembly & Decompilation
courses.summary: Reverse engineer game binaries with Ghidra and IDA: x86-64 calling conventions, function prologues, virtual method tables (VMT), and pattern signature scanning.
courses.expected: Compiles with C++17 (`g++ -std=c++17 mod-reverse-engineering.cpp`). Output shows inspection of the monster's vtable, successful VMT shadow hooking intercepting `takeDamage`, reducing damage to 0, and finding an instruction signature using pattern scanning with wildcards.

lessons.title: Disassembly patterns & x86-64 assembly
paragraphs: Static analysis begins by loading game binaries into disassemblers like Ghidra, IDA Pro, or Binary Ninja. The disassembler converts raw machine bytes into x86-64 assembly mnemonics. Modders quickly learn to recognize standard function structures: the function prologue (allocating the stack frame and preserving registers), the function body, and the epilogue (`ret`).

In 64-bit binaries, compilers use RIP-relative addressing (relative to the instruction pointer) for accessing global variables and string literals (`mov rax, [rip + 0x12345]`). To reconstruct the target address, a modder calculates: `Target = CurrentInstructionAddress + InstructionLength + Displacement`.
lessons.example: push rbp; mov rbp, rsp; sub rsp, 0x40; ... ; mov rax, [rip + 0x2A10]; ... ; add rsp, 0x40; pop rbp; ret;
lessons.pitfall: Assuming stack frame sizes are uniform across compiler optimization levels; release builds often omit frame pointers (`-fomit-frame-pointer`) and reorder instructions aggressively.

question.prompt: How does RIP-relative addressing locate global variables in 64-bit x86-64 binaries?

options.text: By querying a centralized cloud DNS server
By adding a signed 32-bit displacement to the address of the next machine instruction
By resetting the CPU accumulators on every loop iteration

question.explanation: RIP-relative addressing computes target locations as a relative offset from the RIP register (the address of the next sequential instruction).

lessons.title: Calling conventions & ABIs
paragraphs: Calling conventions dictate how parameters are passed to functions, how return values are received, and who cleans up the call stack. On 64-bit Windows, the Microsoft x64 calling convention passes the first four integer/pointer arguments in `RCX, RDX, R8, R9` (with `XMM0-XMM3` for floating-point values) and requires a 32-byte shadow space (homing space) allocated on the stack.

In C++ non-static member functions (`__thiscall`), the implicit `this` pointer pointing to the current object instance is always passed as the first argument (in `RCX` on Windows, or `RDI` on Linux System V AMD64). Modders writing native hook functions must match the target function's exact calling convention, parameter types, and register layout, or the stack will become corrupted upon return.
lessons.example: Windows x64: rcx = this, rdx = param1, r8 = param2, r9 = param3; return value in rax.
lessons.pitfall: Calling a member function without passing the valid object instance in the `this` register causes an instant crash when the function attempts to access member variables.

question.prompt: In the Microsoft 64-bit calling convention, which CPU register receives the implicit 'this' pointer when calling a C++ member function?

options.text: RCX
RAX

question.explanation: On 64-bit Windows, the first argument (which is the implicit `this` pointer in C++ member functions) is passed in `RCX`.

lessons.title: Virtual method tables (VMT / Vtable)
paragraphs: C++ implements dynamic polymorphism via Virtual Method Tables (VMTs). Any class containing virtual functions has an implicit pointer (`vptr`) placed as its very first 64-bit field. The `vptr` points to an array of function pointers stored in the read-only `.rdata` section of the binary.

To intercept virtual function calls, modders use Virtual Method Table Hooking. In VMT Shadowing, the mod allocates a heap copy of the target class's vtable array, replaces specific function pointers with custom hook functions, and overwrites the object's `vptr` to point to the shadow table. Because this technique avoids modifying the game's original `.rdata` section, it easily evades page-integrity anti-cheat scans.
lessons.example: vptr = *(uintptr_t**)object; originalFn = vptr[methodIndex]; shadowVtable[methodIndex] = &myHook; *(uintptr_t*)object = &shadowVtable;
lessons.pitfall: Overwriting function pointers directly inside the original vtable without calling VirtualProtect triggers an access violation because the vtable resides in read-only memory.

question.prompt: What advantage does VMT Shadow Hooking provide over directly overwriting pointers in the original vtable?

options.text: It leaves the original read-only .rdata code section untouched, avoiding memory integrity detection
It automatically converts 32-bit executables into 64-bit binaries
It removes all assembly instructions from the target game

question.explanation: Shadow vtables reside on the mod's own heap, leaving original module memory completely unmodified and clean against checksum scanners.

lessons.title: Pattern scanning & byte signatures
paragraphs: When a game updates or patches, compiler optimizations re-align functions, shifting memory offsets and making hardcoded RVAs obsolete. To build resilient mods that survive game updates, modders use Pattern Scanning (Array of Bytes / AoB scanning).

A pattern signature is a unique sequence of machine code bytes representing a function's prologue or unique instruction sequence. Bytes that change between builds (such as memory offsets, global addresses, or register indices) are designated as wildcards (`?`). At startup, the mod scans the game's executable memory for the pattern and dynamically resolves the function's new address.
lessons.example: Signature: "48 8B 05 ? ? ? ? 48 85 C0 74 12" (wildcards match any bytes in relative displacements).
lessons.pitfall: Choosing a pattern signature that is too short can produce false-positive matches elsewhere in the executable.

question.prompt: Why do pattern scanners use wildcard bytes ('?') in signature strings?

options.text: To skip variable offsets and addresses that change across game updates or builds
To tell the CPU to execute random instructions
Because C++ string literals cannot store hex characters

question.explanation: Wildcards allow signatures to match fixed opcode instructions while ignoring variable displacement bytes that change when the game is recompiled.

courses.title: 4. Native Code Injection & API Hooking
courses.summary: Implement native DLL injection, inline 64-bit detour hooks, trampoline generation, memory protection toggling, and graphics swapchain interception.
courses.expected: Compiles with C++17 (`g++ -std=c++17 mod-native-hooking.cpp`). Output shows the unhooked damage calculation returning 40, the hooked execution intercepting the call and returning 120 (3x critical buff) via the trampoline, followed by clean unhooking and return to 40.

lessons.title: DLL injection mechanisms
paragraphs: Native modding begins with DLL injection, the process of forcing a target game process to load a dynamic link library authored by the modder. Once inside the game's address space, the DLL shares the game's virtual memory, privileges, and thread execution contexts.

Common injection methods include `CreateRemoteThread` with `LoadLibrary` (writing the DLL path into the target process and triggering a remote thread), Windows hook injection via `SetWindowsHookEx`, and Manual Mapping. Manual mapping parses the PE header, maps sections into memory, resolves import address tables (IAT), and executes the entry point manually, evading tools that monitor `LoadLibrary` events.
lessons.example: HANDLE hThread = CreateRemoteThread(hProcess, NULL, 0, (LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE)LoadLibraryA, remoteStr, 0, NULL);
lessons.pitfall: Using standard CreateRemoteThread in games with anti-cheat software immediately triggers injection alerts because anti-cheats hook or block OpenProcess handles.

question.prompt: What distinguishes Manual Mapping injection from standard LoadLibrary injection?

options.text: Manual mapping resolves imports and maps PE sections manually without registering the DLL in the OS loaded module list
Manual mapping only works on floppy disks
Manual mapping requires rebooting the computer into safe mode

question.explanation: Manual mapping avoids OS loader APIs, preventing the mod DLL from appearing in the process PEB (Process Environment Block) module list.

lessons.title: Inline hooking & trampolines
paragraphs: Inline hooking (also known as detour hooking) intercepts a function by overwriting its first few machine instructions (the prologue) with an unconditional jump instruction targeting the mod's hook function. When the game calls the function, control transfers immediately to the mod.

To allow the mod to invoke the original game functionality without infinite recursion, the hook engine constructs a 'trampoline'. The trampoline is a dynamically allocated executable buffer containing the stolen prologue instructions followed by an unconditional jump back into the original function immediately after the overwritten hook bytes.
lessons.example: Game Function: [JMP Hook] -> Hook Function executes -> [JMP Trampoline] -> Trampoline: [Stolen Prologue] -> [JMP Game + Offset].
lessons.pitfall: Overwriting a partial instruction when writing a 5-byte or 14-byte jump corrupts adjacent instructions, causing the CPU to execute illegal opcodes and crash.

question.prompt: What is the function of a 'trampoline' in inline detour hooking?

options.text: It executes the original stolen prologue instructions and jumps back to the original function, avoiding infinite recursion
It compresses the game's audio assets
It shuts down the operating system when the game closes

question.explanation: A trampoline preserves the overwritten prologue bytes and jumps back to the original function body, enabling the hook to call the original logic safely.

lessons.title: 64-bit far jumps & memory allocation
paragraphs: In 32-bit x86 systems, an unconditional relative jump instruction (`E9 xx xx xx xx`) requires only 5 bytes and can reach anywhere in the 4 GB address space. In 64-bit systems, relative jumps are limited to a signed 32-bit offset (within ±2 GB of the current RIP). Because the 64-bit address space spans 128 TB, jumping further requires either a 14-byte absolute jump (`FF 25 00 00 00 00 [8-byte address]`) or a nearby relay trampoline.

Hooking libraries (such as MinHook and Detours) scan memory pages within ±2 GB of the target function to allocate 5-byte relay stubs, minimizing the number of prologue bytes that must be overwritten. If a function is shorter than 14 bytes, an absolute jump cannot fit without clobbering adjacent functions.
Modders must also flush the CPU instruction cache with `FlushInstructionCache` after modifying code bytes to ensure multi-core processors do not execute stale cached instructions.
lessons.example: 14-byte jump: FF 25 00 00 00 00 <64-bit target address>; 5-byte jump: E9 <32-bit RIP-relative offset>.
lessons.pitfall: Failing to flush the CPU instruction cache (`FlushInstructionCache`) leads to multi-core synchronization issues where some CPU cores execute old instructions while others execute the new jump.

question.prompt: Why can a standard 5-byte relative jump (E9) instruction fail to reach a hook function in 64-bit processes?

options.text: The 32-bit relative displacement in the E9 opcode can only branch within ±2 GB of the current instruction pointer

courses.title: 5. Managed Modding: Unity, C# & BepInEx
courses.summary: Mod Unity engine games running Mono or IL2CPP: decompile assemblies with dnSpy/ILSpy, build BepInEx 5 plugins, bind persistent configs, and draw in-game IMGUI overlays.
courses.expected: Compiles with modern C# (`csc` or `dotnet run`). Demonstrates the BepInEx lifecycle: plugin initialization in `Awake()`, dynamic hotkey detection in `Update()`, and UI menu rendering in `OnGUI()`.

lessons.title: Unity architecture: Mono vs IL2CPP
paragraphs: Unity games compile game logic through one of two backends: Mono or IL2CPP. In the Mono scripting backend, C# code is compiled into standard Common Intermediate Language (CIL) bytecode packaged into `.dll` files (predominantly `Assembly-CSharp.dll`). When the game runs, the Mono runtime Just-In-Time (JIT) compiles bytecode into machine code.

In the IL2CPP (Intermediate Language to C++) backend, Unity converts CIL bytecode into native C++ source code before compiling it directly into a native platform binary (`GameAssembly.dll`). While Mono games are trivial to decompile and modify, IL2CPP games require metadata restoration tools (such as Il2CppDumper or Cpp2IL) to recover class definitions and method signatures.
lessons.example: Mono: Managed assemblies in `Managed/Assembly-CSharp.dll`. IL2CPP: Native `GameAssembly.dll` paired with `global-metadata.dat`.
lessons.pitfall: Attempting to open an IL2CPP game's `GameAssembly.dll` in a C# decompiler like dnSpy will fail because it contains native machine code, not CIL bytecode.

question.explanation: In Unity Mono builds, the game's custom scripts and game logic are compiled into `Assembly-CSharp.dll` inside the `Managed` directory.

lessons.title: Decompiling managed binaries with dnSpy
paragraphs: Because CIL bytecode retains rich metadata—including type names, field names, method signatures, and parameter labels—managed Unity games can be decompiled back into nearly original C# source code using tools like dnSpy, ILSpy, or dotPeek.

Using dnSpy, a modder can open `Assembly-CSharp.dll`, search for terms like `PlayerHealth`, `TakeDamage`, or `AddCurrency`, read the exact C# implementation, set breakpoints for live debugging, or directly edit IL instructions. This provides total visibility into game mechanics without having to guess struct offsets.
lessons.example: Opening Assembly-CSharp.dll -> Searching for 'CalculateSpeed' -> Inspecting original C# implementation and class variables.
lessons.pitfall: Modifying and recompiling `Assembly-CSharp.dll` directly on disk breaks mod interoperability, as multiple mods cannot overwrite the same DLL without overwriting each other.

question.prompt: Why can C# Unity Mono games be decompiled into high-level readable source code so easily?

Unity automatically uploads the developer's original C# source code to GitHub
Managed games do not use compiled code

question.explanation: CIL bytecode is a high-level intermediate representation containing comprehensive metadata, allowing decompilers to reconstruct the original C# code structure.

lessons.title: BepInEx plugin architecture
paragraphs: BepInEx (Bepis Injector Extensible) is the industry-standard mod loader for Unity games across both Mono and IL2CPP runtimes. BepInEx acts as a bootstrap hook by placing a custom `winhttp.dll` or `version.dll` in the game root, hijacking the OS DLL search order during game launch.

Once loaded, BepInEx initializes a plugin manager that scans the `BepInEx/plugins` folder for mod assemblies. Every BepInEx mod inherits from `BaseUnityPlugin` and specifies metadata using the `[BepInPlugin("guid", "name", "version")]` attribute. Plugins participate in standard Unity MonoBehaviour lifecycles (`Awake`, `Start`, `Update`, `OnGUI`).
lessons.example: [BepInPlugin("com.author.mymod", "MyMod", "1.0.0")] public class MyMod : BaseUnityPlugin { void Awake() { ... } }
lessons.pitfall: Omitting the `[BepInPlugin]` attribute prevents BepInEx from recognizing the class as an active plugin, resulting in the mod failing to load.

question.prompt: How does BepInEx ensure its mod loader executes when the Unity game starts up?

options.text: By placing a proxy DLL (such as winhttp.dll) in the game root to exploit OS DLL search order hijacking
By editing the computer's motherboard BIOS firmware
By executing a background cloud cron job

question.explanation: BepInEx uses proxy DLLs like `winhttp.dll` in the game folder, which the game executable loads automatically before loading standard system DLLs.

lessons.title: Configuration systems & IMGUI overlays
paragraphs: High-quality mods allow players to customize gameplay settings through configuration files rather than requiring code edits. BepInEx provides a built-in configuration manager via `Config.Bind<T>(section, key, defaultValue, description)`, which automatically generates and synchronizes a clean `.cfg` file under `BepInEx/config`.

For in-game interfaces, Unity mods frequently utilize Unity's legacy Immediate Mode GUI (`OnGUI`) system. `OnGUI` is invoked multiple times per frame, allowing modders to draw windows (`GUI.Window`), labels (`GUI.Label`), and buttons (`GUI.Button`) with zero external asset dependencies or canvas setups.
lessons.example: var speed = Config.Bind("Player", "Speed", 5.0f, "Movement speed"); void OnGUI() { if (GUI.Button(new Rect(10,10,100,30), "Boost")) { ... } }
lessons.pitfall: Creating new texture or font resources inside `OnGUI` leaks memory rapidly because `OnGUI` executes dozens of times per second.

options.text: It can be rendered directly from code without needing Unity Editor prefabs, asset bundles, or Canvas hierarchy setups
It runs exclusively on 3dfx Voodoo graphics cards

question.explanation: OnGUI allows UI buttons, boxes, and text to be drawn purely through code statements in `BaseUnityPlugin`, requiring no external prefab assets.

courses.title: 6. Dynamic Runtime Patching with Harmony
courses.summary: Master the Harmony patching library: intercept methods with Prefix short-circuiting, modify return values with Postfix and ref __result, and manipulate CIL opcodes using Transpilers.
courses.expected: Compiles with modern C#. Output demonstrates unpatched damage calculation (20 damage, durability drops to 90), followed by Harmony Prefix altering armor and critical hit flags, and Harmony Postfix buffing final damage to 125, ending with a simulated CIL Transpiler replacing the durability opcode.

lessons.title: The Harmony patching framework
paragraphs: Harmony is an open-source library that allows C# developers to alter and extend methods in third-party .NET applications and Unity games at runtime. Unlike traditional modding approaches that patch DLL files on disk, Harmony injects modifications dynamically in process memory using DynamicMethod and JIT compilation.

Because Harmony does not alter files on disk, multiple independent mods can patch the same method simultaneously. Harmony maintains an internal patch registry, chaining prefixes, transpilers, and postfixes from multiple mods into a unified, conflict-free runtime wrapper.
lessons.example: var harmony = new Harmony("com.myname.mod"); harmony.PatchAll();
lessons.pitfall: Modifying assembly files on disk while Harmony is active creates duplicate patch conflicts and breaks game integrity checks.

question.prompt: What major advantage does Harmony offer when multiple different mods need to alter the same game function?

options.text: Harmony coordinates runtime patches from multiple mods without them overwriting the physical DLL file on disk
Harmony deletes all other mods automatically
Harmony forces all mods to run in single-threaded mode

question.explanation: Harmony chains multiple patches together in memory at runtime, allowing numerous mods to extend the same method without disk conflicts.

lessons.title: Prefix patches & short-circuiting
paragraphs: A Harmony Prefix patch executes before the original target method begins. Prefixes are annotated with `[HarmonyPrefix]`. They can read the invoking object instance via `__instance`, inspect and alter incoming arguments using the `ref` keyword, and store state across to the postfix using `__state`.

A critical feature of Prefix patches is 'short-circuiting'. If a Prefix method returns `bool`, returning `true` allows the original method to proceed normally. However, returning `false` skips the original method completely, allowing the mod to substitute custom logic or prevent an event entirely (such as blocking player death or cancelling a weapon cooldown).
lessons.example: static bool Prefix(ref int damage) { if (GodMode) return false; damage *= 2; return true; }
lessons.pitfall: Returning false in a Prefix without setting `ref __result` for non-void methods causes the method to return default uninitialized values (such as null or 0).

question.prompt: What happens when a Harmony Prefix method returns false?

options.text: The original game method is skipped (short-circuited), jumping directly to postfixes
The game crashes immediately with an unhandled exception
The computer restarts

question.explanation: Returning false from a boolean Prefix prevents the original game method from running, effectively replacing its execution with the mod's logic.

lessons.title: Postfix patches & result modification
paragraphs: A Harmony Postfix patch executes immediately after the original target method finishes. Postfixes are annotated with `[HarmonyPostfix]`. Because the original method has already executed, Postfixes are ideal for reacting to completed events, logging outcomes, or modifying the return value.

To modify what the caller receives from the method, the Postfix includes a parameter named `ref __result` matching the method's return type. For example, if a game function `CalculateSellPrice()` returns `100`, a Postfix can alter `__result = __result * 2` to grant double gold to the merchant.
lessons.example: static void Postfix(ref int __result) { __result = (int)(__result * 1.5f); }
lessons.pitfall: Attempting to change incoming method arguments inside a Postfix has no effect on the method's calculations because the method has already completed.

question.prompt: How does a Harmony Postfix patch modify the return value of a game method?

options.text: By accepting a parameter named ref __result and assigning a new value to it
By editing the Windows pagefile
By calling Console.ReadLine()

question.explanation: Harmony recognizes the special parameter `ref __result` and passes the method's return value by reference so the Postfix can modify it.

lessons.title: Transpilers & CIL instruction rewriting
paragraphs: Transpilers are the most surgical and performant type of Harmony patch. Instead of wrapping a method in prefix/postfix logic, a Transpiler receives the method's raw Common Intermediate Language (CIL) instruction stream (`IEnumerable<CodeInstruction>`), rewrites specific opcodes, and emits a modified instruction list before the method is JIT-compiled.

Using Transpilers, a modder can replace a single numeric constant (e.g. replacing `ldc.i4.s 10` with `ldc.i4.0` to disable stamina consumption), insert new method calls (`call` or `callvirt`), or redirect conditional branch jumps. Because changes are baked directly into the JIT-compiled machine code, Transpilers incur zero runtime function call overhead.
lessons.example: if (instruction.opcode == OpCodes.Ldc_I4_5) yield return new CodeInstruction(OpCodes.Ldc_I4, 20);
lessons.pitfall: Emitting an invalid sequence of CIL instructions that desynchronizes the evaluation stack results in an `InvalidProgramException` when the CLR attempts to JIT-compile the method.

question.prompt: Why are Harmony Transpilers considered more performant than heavy Prefix/Postfix wrappers for small logic tweaks?

options.text: They rewrite CIL instructions before JIT compilation, resulting in optimized native code with zero wrapper call overhead
They run directly on the graphics card without using the CPU
They disable .NET garbage collection entirely

question.explanation: Transpilers modify the bytecode instructions directly prior to JIT compilation, eliminating the call overhead of external wrapper methods.

courses.title: 7. Unreal Engine Modding & Reflection Systems
courses.summary: Explore Unreal Engine 4/5 reflection: UObject hierarchies, GUObjectArray iteration, universal ProcessEvent hooking, C++ SDK generation, and UE4SS scripting.
courses.expected: Compiles with C++17 (`g++ -std=c++17 mod-unreal-engine.cpp`). Demonstrates Unreal Engine reflection, iterating `GUObjectArray`, and hooking `ProcessEvent` to intercept `ReceiveDamage` calls, successfully neutralizing lethal player damage to 0.

lessons.title: Unreal reflection: UObject, UClass & UFunction
paragraphs: Unreal Engine is built upon a proprietary, high-performance C++ reflection system. Because native C++ lacks built-in runtime reflection, Epic's Unreal Header Tool (UHT) parses macros (`UCLASS()`, `UFUNCTION()`, `UPROPERTY()`) during compilation to generate metadata structs describing every class, method, property, and memory offset.

Every reflected entity inherits from `UObject`. A `UClass` describes an object's type and contains a linked list of fields (`FProperty`) and functions (`UFunction`). By reading this reflection metadata at runtime, modders can discover private variables, inspect struct offsets, and invoke engine functions without needing game source code.
lessons.example: UObject* obj = GUObjectArray->FindObject("BP_Hero_C"); UFunction* fn = obj->Class->FindFunctionByName("SetInvincible");
lessons.pitfall: Attempting to access non-reflected C++ classes through the reflection system will fail because only entities marked with `UCLASS()` are tracked in the reflection tables.

question.explanation: In Unreal Engine, all reflected classes, components, functions, and blueprints derive from `UObject`.

lessons.title: GUObjectArray & runtime object discovery
paragraphs: All active `UObject` instances in an Unreal Engine game are registered in a global array known as `GUObjectArray`. The array is divided into fixed chunks (typically 65,536 objects per chunk) to avoid large single-heap reallocations during gameplay.

Modders locate `GUObjectArray` via AoB pattern scanning at startup. By iterating through the array, a mod can locate the active `GWorld`, find the local `APlayerController`, enumerate all spawned enemy actors, or dump the game's entire class hierarchy into complete C++ SDK headers.
lessons.example: for (int i = 0; i < GUObjectArray->GetObjectArrayNum(); ++i) { UObject* obj = GUObjectArray->GetObjectPtr(i); }
lessons.pitfall: Dereferencing entries in GUObjectArray without checking the object's `Flags` for `RF_PendingKill` or `RF_BeginDestroyed` leads to access violations on garbage-collected objects.

question.prompt: What is the primary role of GUObjectArray in Unreal Engine modding?

options.text: It provides a global lookup table of all active UObject instances, allowing modders to discover actors and reflection data at runtime
It handles sound card mixing for Dolby Atmos
It compiles C++ source files into Python bytecode

question.explanation: GUObjectArray tracks every instantiated UObject in memory, making it the gateway for discovering world state, players, and classes.

lessons.title: The ProcessEvent hook
paragraphs: In Unreal Engine, `UObject::ProcessEvent(UFunction* Function, void* Parms)` is the universal execution bridge between native C++ and Blueprint scripting. Whenever a Blueprint node executes, an animation notify triggers, or a networked RPC arrives, the engine calls `ProcessEvent`.

Because nearly all high-level gameplay passes through this single function, hooking `ProcessEvent` provides unprecedented modding leverage. A single detour hook on `ProcessEvent` can log every function call in the game, intercept input commands, modify damage calculations, or cancel unwanted gameplay events entirely.
lessons.example: void HookedProcessEvent(UObject* context, UFunction* function, void* parms) { if (function->GetName() == "Die") return; Original(context, function, parms); }
lessons.pitfall: Adding heavy string comparisons or logging to every `ProcessEvent` call tanks performance because the engine calls `ProcessEvent` thousands of times per second.

question.prompt: Why is hooking UObject::ProcessEvent considered the most powerful single hook in Unreal Engine modding?

options.text: Nearly all Blueprint functions, animation notifies, and gameplay events pass through ProcessEvent, enabling universal interception
It unlocks hidden graphics settings in the monitor hardware
It automatically translates game audio into text

question.explanation: ProcessEvent is the central dispatcher for Unreal's Blueprint virtual machine and reflected RPCs, making it a universal interception point.

lessons.title: SDK generation & UE4SS
paragraphs: Reverse engineering every struct offset by hand is tedious. Instead, modders use SDK Generators (or tools like UE4SS - Unreal Engine 4/5 Scripting System) that traverse `GUObjectArray`, read `FProperty` offsets, and automatically generate compilable C++ header files reflecting the exact classes of the game.

UE4SS also embeds a Lua scripting engine directly into Unreal Engine games. Modders can author Lua scripts that bind to `UFunction` hooks, query `UObject` instances, and spawn custom Blueprint mods without writing or compiling a single line of C++.
lessons.example: UE4SS Lua hook: RegisterHook("/Script/Engine.PlayerController:ClientTravel", function(self, URL) print(URL) end)
lessons.pitfall: Using an SDK generated from an older version of a game causes memory offset shifts if the game developers added or reordered class properties.

Reinstalls the operating system

question.explanation: An SDK generator iterates the engine's reflection structures and outputs accurate C++ headers with correct member offsets and virtual functions.

lessons.title: Why games embed Lua scripting
paragraphs: Many of the most moddable games in history—including World of Warcraft, Factorio, Civilization, Garry's Mod, and Don't Starve—embed Lua as their scripting language. Lua is ultra-lightweight (entire compiler and VM under 300 KB), extremely fast, and designed from the ground up for seamless embedding inside host C and C++ engines.

By decoupling high-level game logic (quests, item definitions, UI behaviors, skill balancing) from the compiled C++ core, game designers and community modders can alter mechanics, iterate on designs, and reload scripts instantly without recompiling the executable.

lessons.pitfall: Executing complex tight loops (like pathfinding over thousands of nodes) in Lua can cause noticeable CPU bottlenecks compared to native C++ implementations.

lessons.title: The Lua C API & virtual stack
paragraphs: Communication between the host C++ application and the Lua interpreter occurs through a shared virtual stack managed by `lua_State*`. Every function argument, return value, table access, and string passes through this stack.

Stack indexing operates in two directions: positive indices reference elements from the bottom of the stack up (`1` is the first element pushed), while negative indices reference elements from the top down (`-1` is the most recent element pushed). Functions adhere to strict stack discipline: C functions pop their inputs and return the exact count of return values pushed.
lessons.example: lua_pushnumber(L, 42.0); lua_pushstring(L, "hero"); // -1 is "hero", -2 is 42.0
lessons.pitfall: Failing to balance the Lua stack by pushing values without popping them causes stack overflow crashes over extended gameplay sessions.

question.prompt: In the Lua C API, what does a stack index of -1 represent?

options.text: The top element of the stack (the most recently pushed value)
An invalid error code indicating out-of-memory
The bottom-most element of the stack

question.explanation: Negative indices index from the top of the stack downwards, where -1 is always the topmost (latest) item.

lessons.title: Exposing engine functions to Lua
paragraphs: To allow mods to interact with the game world, the host engine registers native C functions with the Lua environment using `lua_register` or `lua_pushcfunction`. Functions must conform to the `lua_CFunction` typedef: `int (*lua_CFunction)(lua_State *L)`.

Inside the registered C function, the developer reads arguments from the stack using functions like `lua_tointeger` or `lua_tostring`, performs the engine logic (e.g. spawns an entity or changes player health), pushes any result values back onto the stack, and returns an integer specifying how many results were pushed.
lessons.example: int MySpawn(lua_State* L) { const char* name = lua_tostring(L, 1); SpawnActor(name); return 0; }
lessons.pitfall: Assuming arguments passed from Lua are valid without calling type check functions (`lua_isstring`, `lua_isnumber`) causes memory corruption if a script passes unexpected types.

question.prompt: What does the integer return value of a lua_CFunction represent?

options.text: The number of return values the function pushed onto the Lua stack for the caller
The execution time in milliseconds
The exit status code of the operating system

question.explanation: In the Lua C API, the integer returned by a C-function tells the Lua runtime how many values on the stack should be returned to the script.

lessons.title: Sandboxing & event dispatch
paragraphs: When allowing players to download community mods from mod repositories or Steam Workshop, security is paramount. A malicious mod script could attempt to read private user files, download malware, or execute arbitrary OS shell commands using standard Lua libraries.

Engine developers enforce sandboxing by stripping dangerous standard packages—specifically `io` (file access), `os` (command execution), `package` (loading arbitrary C modules), and `debug`. The game provides custom, safe replacement APIs and dispatches events via registered callback tables (e.g., `events.on_player_damaged`).
lessons.example: lua_pushnil(L); lua_setglobal(L, "os"); // Removes the OS package completely
lessons.pitfall: Leaving the `debug` library enabled in sandboxed Lua environments allows malicious scripts to extract upvalues and escape the sandbox environment.

To reduce electricity consumption by the GPU

question.explanation: Sandboxing strips unsafe capabilities like file I/O and process execution, ensuring downloaded mods cannot compromise the player's system.

courses.title: 9. Asset Pipelines, PAK Archives & Save Game Engineering
courses.summary: Extract, modify, and repack game assets: Unreal PAK / Unity AssetBundles, texture and audio replacement, binary save file deserialization, and CRC32 checksum recalculation.
courses.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Asset Pipeline & Save File Engineering Utility (Python 3)
# Demonstrates unpacking/repacking custom PAK archives with zlib compression,
# and deserializing binary game save data with CRC32 integrity checksum recalculation.

import struct
import zlib
import binascii

class PakArchive:
    """
    Custom PAK format:
    [Header: 4 bytes Magic 'VPAK', 4 bytes FileCount]
    [Index Table: For each file: 32 bytes Name, 4 bytes Offset, 4 bytes CompressedSize, 4 bytes UncompressedSize]
    [Payload Data: Compressed byte payloads]
    """
    MAGIC = b'VPAK'

    @staticmethod
    def pack(files_dict: dict) -> bytes:
        file_count = len(files_dict)
        header = struct.pack('<4sI', PakArchive.MAGIC, file_count)

        index_entries = []
        payload_data = bytearray()
        
        # Calculate start of payload data
        index_size = file_count * (32 + 4 + 4 + 4)
        current_offset = len(header) + index_size

        for name, data in files_dict.items():
            compressed = zlib.compress(data)
            comp_size = len(compressed)
            uncomp_size = len(data)
            
            # Pad name to 32 bytes
            name_bytes = name.encode('utf-8')[:32].ljust(32, b'\x00')
            index_entries.append(struct.pack('<32sIII', name_bytes, current_offset, comp_size, uncomp_size))
            
            payload_data.extend(compressed)
            current_offset += comp_size

        return header + b''.join(index_entries) + bytes(payload_data)

    @staticmethod
    def unpack(archive_bytes: bytes) -> dict:
        magic, file_count = struct.unpack_from('<4sI', archive_bytes, 0)
        if magic != PakArchive.MAGIC:
            raise ValueError("Invalid archive magic header")

        offset = 8
        files = {}
        for _ in range(file_count):
            name_raw, file_offset, comp_size, uncomp_size = struct.unpack_from('<32sIII', archive_bytes, offset)
            name = name_raw.decode('utf-8').rstrip('\x00')
            
            compressed_data = archive_bytes[file_offset:file_offset + comp_size]
            decompressed_data = zlib.decompress(compressed_data)
            files[name] = decompressed_data
            
            offset += (32 + 4 + 4 + 4)

        return files


class SaveGameManager:
    """
    Binary Save Format:
    [4 bytes Magic 'VQSV']
    [4 bytes PlayerLevel]
    [4 bytes PlayerXP]
    [4 bytes PlayerGold]
    [4 bytes CRC32 Checksum of preceding fields]
    """
    MAGIC = b'VQSV'

    @staticmethod
    def create_save(level: int, xp: int, gold: int) -> bytes:
        payload = struct.pack('<4sIII', SaveGameManager.MAGIC, level, xp, gold)
        checksum = binascii.crc32(payload) & 0xFFFFFFFF
        return payload + struct.pack('<I', checksum)

    @staticmethod
    def read_and_verify(save_bytes: bytes) -> dict:
        if len(save_bytes) != 20:
            raise ValueError("Corrupt save file length")

        payload = save_bytes[:16]
        expected_crc = struct.unpack('<I', save_bytes[16:20])[0]
        actual_crc = binascii.crc32(payload) & 0xFFFFFFFF

        if actual_crc != expected_crc:
            raise ValueError(f"Save file corrupted or tampered! CRC mismatch: expected {expected_crc:#010x}, got {actual_crc:#010x}")

        magic, level, xp, gold = struct.unpack('<4sIII', payload)
        return {"level": level, "xp": xp, "gold": gold, "crc": hex(expected_crc)}

    @staticmethod
    def modify_gold(save_bytes: bytes, new_gold: int) -> bytes:
        magic, level, xp, _ = struct.unpack('<4sIII', save_bytes[:16])
        new_payload = struct.pack('<4sIII', magic, level, xp, new_gold)
        new_crc = binascii.crc32(new_payload) & 0xFFFFFFFF
        return new_payload + struct.pack('<I', new_crc)


def main():
    print("=== Asset Pipeline & Save File Engineering Demo ===\n")

    # 1. Test PAK archive packing & unpacking
    original_assets = {
        "textures/player_skin.png": b"FAKE_TEXTURE_DATA_PNG_BYTES_8888",
        "configs/game_balance.json": b'{"hero_speed": 10.0, "gravity": 9.8}',
        "audio/laser_blast.wav": b"RIFF....WAVEfmt ....data..."
    }

    print("[PAK] Packing 3 assets into compressed archive...")
    pak_blob = PakArchive.pack(original_assets)
    print(f"[PAK] Created archive size: {len(pak_blob)} bytes")

    print("[PAK] Unpacking archive and inspecting balance config...")
    unpacked = PakArchive.unpack(pak_blob)
    print(f"[PAK] Extracted config content: {unpacked['configs/game_balance.json'].decode('utf-8')}\n")

    # 2. Test Binary Save Game & Checksum Modification
    print("[SaveEngine] Generating legitimate player save file...")
    legit_save = SaveGameManager.create_save(level=5, xp=1200, gold=250)
    save_info = SaveGameManager.read_and_verify(legit_save)
    print(f"[SaveEngine] Verified save data: Level {save_info['level']}, Gold {save_info['gold']} (CRC: {save_info['crc']})")

    # Tampering test (naive byte edit without updating CRC)
    print("\n[SaveEngine] Simulating naive hex edit (overwriting gold without updating CRC)...")
    tampered_bytes = bytearray(legit_save)
    tampered_bytes[12] = 0xFF # Corrupt gold byte
    try:
        SaveGameManager.read_and_verify(bytes(tampered_bytes))
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"[SaveEngine] Anti-tamper triggered: {e}")

    # Proper Modder Modification (Recalculating CRC32)
    print("\n[SaveEngine] Applying proper mod: Injecting 999,999 gold and recalculating valid CRC32...")
    modded_save = SaveGameManager.modify_gold(legit_save, 999999)
    modded_info = SaveGameManager.read_and_verify(modded_save)
    print(f"[SaveEngine] Successfully modified! New Gold: {modded_info['gold']} (New Valid CRC: {modded_info['crc']})")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

lessons.title: Asset pipelines & virtual filesystems
paragraphs: Modern game engines organize game content (textures, meshes, audio, maps) through virtual filesystem (VFS) layers. Instead of reading directly from hard drive folders, engines query mounting points with prioritized search paths.

Asset modding works by injecting higher-priority mount points. For example, in Unreal Engine, `.pak` files in the `~mods` directory take precedence over base game archives. If a mod archive contains an asset at the exact relative path (`Content/Characters/Hero/Texture.uasset`), the engine loads the modded file without needing to touch original archives.
lessons.example: VFS search order: 1. Game/Mods/*.pak (Priority 100) -> 2. Game/Content/*.pak (Priority 0).
lessons.pitfall: Failing to match the exact internal directory hierarchy and filename of the target asset prevents the VFS from associating the replacement with the original reference.

question.prompt: How do virtual filesystem (VFS) mounting priorities enable asset replacement mods?

options.text: By allowing mod archives with higher mount priorities to intercept file path lookups before base game archives
By compressing all texture files into text documents
By converting 3D meshes into vector fonts

question.explanation: Virtual filesystems check high-priority mount directories (like `~mods`) first, returning the modded asset whenever paths match.

lessons.title: Archive formats & compression
paragraphs: To minimize file fragmentation, load times, and disk space, games package thousands of individual files into monolithic archive containers (Unreal `.pak` / `.ucas` / `.utoc`, Unity AssetBundles, or custom ZIP containers).

A typical archive contains a header, an index table (recording filenames, offsets, and uncompressed/compressed sizes), and compressed data chunks. Common compression algorithms include zlib (deflate), LZ4 (optimized for lightning-fast decompression), and Zstandard (ZSTD). Understanding the archive header structure is required to unpack, modify, and repack game files.
lessons.example: Archive Header -> Index: [File 'skin.dds', Offset 0x1000, Size 500 KB] -> Payload at 0x1000.
lessons.pitfall: Modifying an extracted file and repacking without recalculating the archive index table offsets causes files to be read from wrong memory boundaries, corrupting the game.

question.prompt: Why must archive repacking tools update the index table offsets when replacing a compressed asset file?

options.text: If the modified asset differs in byte size, all subsequent file offsets in the archive shift and must be updated
Because game engines only accept files with even-numbered byte sizes
To prevent the operating system from deleting the file

question.explanation: Changing a file's compressed size shifts the starting byte offsets of all subsequent files, requiring complete index table reconstruction.

lessons.title: Save file formats: binary vs structured
paragraphs: Game saves preserve player progress across sessions. Games utilize two primary paradigms: human-readable structured formats (JSON, XML, YAML) or binary serialized formats (custom binary structs, Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers).

Binary save files pack raw C/C++ struct bytes directly to disk for speed and compactness. Modding binary saves requires understanding field order, data sizes (e.g. `uint32` vs `float64`), endianness (little-endian on x86/ARM), and struct alignment padding. Using Python's `struct` module allows precise unpacking and packing of binary format layouts.
lessons.example: struct.unpack('<IIf', data[:12]) parses two little-endian unsigned ints and a 32-bit float.
lessons.pitfall: Overlooking struct memory alignment padding (such as 4-byte padding inserted after a 4-byte int before an 8-byte pointer) causes offset alignment errors when editing binary saves.

question.prompt: What Python standard library module is used to pack and unpack raw binary C structs when creating save game editors?

question.explanation: Python's `struct` module translates between Python values and C structs represented as binary byte strings using format characters like `<I` or `<f`.

lessons.title: Checksums, integrity & safe editing
paragraphs: To detect save corruption and prevent casual save file tampering, game developers append integrity checksums or cryptographic hashes (CRC32, Adler-32, MD5, SHA-256) to the end of save files.

When the game loads a save, it recalculates the checksum of the data payload and compares it against the stored checksum. If a modder uses a hex editor to change gold from 100 to 99999 without updating the checksum, the game flags the save as corrupt. Successful save editing tools replicate the checksum algorithm, re-signing the modified payload before saving.
lessons.example: Payload = Level + XP + Gold; ExpectedCRC = crc32(Payload); Compare with saveBytes[16:20].
lessons.pitfall: Failing to exclude the checksum field itself when calculating the checksum hash causes an immediate verification mismatch.

question.prompt: Why does a game report 'Save File Corrupt' after a player changes their gold count using a standard hex editor?

options.text: The stored integrity checksum (such as CRC32) no longer matches the recalculated hash of the altered save data
Hex editors automatically delete save files

question.explanation: Changing values without recalculating the corresponding checksum causes the game's integrity check to fail, triggering corruption alerts.

lessons.title: Production mod architecture
paragraphs: Production-grade game mods require clean, modular architecture. A commercial-quality mod is organized into decoupled layers: the Core Ingestion layer (hooks and memory scanners), the State/Data model, the Feature subsystems (aim assist, camera controls, stat buffs), the UI presentation layer, and the Configuration manager.

Thread synchronization is paramount. The graphics hook runs on the game's render thread, gameplay hooks run on the physics/tick thread, and mod background logic runs on dedicated worker threads. Access to shared state must be protected using mutexes, lock-free queues, or atomic variables to prevent race conditions and intermittent crashes.
lessons.example: Architecture: [DirectX Hook] -> [ImGui Layer] <==> [Atomic Mod Settings] <==> [Detour Hooks on Tick Thread].
lessons.pitfall: Executing expensive memory allocations, file I/O, or blocking network calls directly on the graphics render thread causes noticeable FPS drops and stuttering.

question.prompt: Why must mod settings and commands shared between the render thread and worker threads use atomic variables or mutex locks?

options.text: To prevent concurrent read/write race conditions and data corruption across threads
To ensure colors display with high dynamic range
Because modern operating systems do not allow multiple threads

question.explanation: Synchronizing data access between render threads and worker threads prevents data races, memory corruption, and desynchronization.

lessons.title: In-game overlays with Dear ImGui
paragraphs: Dear ImGui is the undisputed industry standard for creating in-game developer menus, mod settings overlays, and debug tools. ImGui is an immediate-mode C++ GUI library designed to be rendered directly inside existing 3D graphics swapchains (DirectX 9/11/12, Vulkan, OpenGL, Metal).

To enable keyboard and mouse interaction with the mod overlay without clicking through into the game, modders hook the game's window message handler (`WndProc`). When the mod menu is open, the hooked `WndProc` forwards mouse coordinates and key events to ImGui with `ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler` and blocks the message from reaching the underlying game.
lessons.example: LRESULT CALLBACK HookedWndProc(HWND hWnd, UINT uMsg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { if (ImGuiOpen && ImGui_ImplWin32(hWnd, uMsg, wParam, lParam)) return 1; return CallWindowProc(OriginalWndProc, hWnd, uMsg, wParam, lParam); }
lessons.pitfall: Failing to pass input messages back to the original game `WndProc` when the mod menu is closed freezes the player's mouse and keyboard controls completely.

question.prompt: How do game mods capture mouse and keyboard inputs for Dear ImGui menus without triggering in-game actions like firing weapons?

options.text: By hooking the window procedure (WndProc) and intercepting input messages when the mod menu is open
By disconnecting the player's physical keyboard
By pausing the computer's CPU clock

question.explanation: Hooking the window procedure (WndProc) allows the mod to intercept Windows mouse/keyboard messages and consume them before the game receives them.

lessons.title: Crash resilience & exception handling
paragraphs: A mod that crashes the game ruins the player's experience. In native C++, dereferencing an invalid or null pointer triggers a hardware access violation (code `0xC0000005`). Standard C++ `try/catch(...)` blocks do not catch hardware access violations on Windows.

To make hooks resilient against invalid pointers during loading screens or unexpected game states, modders wrap memory-reading code in Structured Exception Handling (`__try / __except` on Windows) or register vectored exception handlers (`AddVectoredExceptionHandler`). If an invalid address is read, the exception handler catches it cleanly, logs an error, and prevents the game process from crashing.
lessons.example: __try { float hp = *(float*)(actor + 0x120); } __except (EXCEPTION_EXECUTE_HANDLER) { LogError("Invalid actor pointer"); }
lessons.pitfall: Using SEH to hide persistent bugs instead of fixing underlying null pointer validations leads to undefined behavior and corrupted state over time.

question.prompt: Why is Windows Structured Exception Handling (__try / __except) used in native mod hooks?

options.text: It catches hardware access violations (like reading null or invalid pointers) that standard C++ try/catch blocks miss, preventing process crashes
It accelerates CPU clock frequencies
It compresses compiled binaries into ZIP archives

question.explanation: Structured Exception Handling (SEH) catches OS-level hardware exceptions like access violations (0xC0000005), preventing crashes during pointer dereferencing.

lessons.title: Mod distribution, packaging & versioning
paragraphs: Publishing a mod for the public requires packaging according to community mod manager standards (Nexus Mods, Thunderstore, CurseForge, Steam Workshop). Standard distribution packages include the compiled mod binary, a `manifest.json` describing dependencies and versioning, default configuration files, and an informative `README.md`.

Mods must follow Semantic Versioning (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`). A major bump indicates breaking changes (such as new save file formats or incompatible config files); minor bumps introduce backward-compatible features; patch bumps resolve bugs. Declaring explicit dependencies in `manifest.json` ensures players install prerequisite mod loaders (like BepInEx or UE4SS) automatically.
lessons.example: manifest.json: { "name": "VoltBoost", "version_number": "1.2.0", "dependencies": ["denikson-BepInExPack-5.4.2100"] }
lessons.pitfall: Distributing original copyrighted game assets inside your mod package violates copyright laws; distribution packages should contain only the modder's code and original creations.

A minor bug fix that changes no features
A simple typo correction in the readme file

question.explanation: Semantic Versioning increments MAJOR version when incompatible API or architecture changes are introduced that break previous versions.
